title: Selecting Textiles & Fabric Construction
description: Woven, non-woven and knitted fabric structures, and how to select textiles by function, aesthetics and sustainability.
content_html:
From Fibre to Yarn to Fabric

Before a fabric can be made, raw fibres must be transformed into yarn. Short staple fibres (such as cotton or cut synthetic staples) are carded to align the fibres, then drawn out and twisted together in a process called spinning. The twist locks the fibres together, giving the yarn strength: the more twist, the stronger but less soft the yarn. Continuous synthetic filaments can be used directly or twisted with other filaments to form a multi-filament yarn. The structure of the yarn — smooth, textured, thick, or fine — influences the drape, feel and appearance of the finished fabric.

Woven Fabrics

A woven fabric is produced on a loom by interlacing two sets of yarns at right angles. The yarns running lengthways are the warp; those running widthways are the weft. The pattern in which warp and weft cross determines the weave structure and the fabric's properties:

  • Plain weave — the weft passes over one warp thread and under the next in a simple alternating pattern. This produces a firm, hard-wearing fabric with no clear right or wrong side. Examples include calico, muslin and many shirting fabrics. Plain weave is the most common weave structure.
  • Twill weave — the weft passes over two (or more) warp threads before going under one, with each row offset by one thread, creating a distinctive diagonal rib on the fabric surface. Twill fabrics are softer, more flexible and more durable than plain weave equivalents. Denim and gabardine are classic twill weaves.
  • Satin weave — the warp floats over four or more weft threads before going under one. These long floats reflect light to create a smooth, lustrous surface. Satin-weave fabrics drape beautifully but snag easily and are less durable than plain or twill weaves. Satin and sateen are typical examples used in evening wear and bed linen.
Key Fact

Woven fabrics are generally stable — they do not stretch significantly (except on the bias, i.e. at 45° to the grain), they fray when cut and they hold their shape well. The tightness of the weave (thread count) affects strength, opacity and feel.

Non-Woven Fabrics

Non-woven fabrics are made directly from fibres or filaments bonded together by mechanical, chemical or thermal means — without spinning into yarn or weaving on a loom. They tend to be cheaper and quicker to manufacture than woven fabrics but are generally weaker and do not drape as well.

  • Bonded/needle-punched non-wovens — fibres are laid in a web and then either punched together with barbed needles (needle punching, which mechanically entangles the fibres) or bonded with heat (thermal bonding, where thermoplastic fibres melt slightly to fuse together) or adhesive chemicals. Products include interfacing (used to stiffen collars and waistbands), disposable medical gowns and geotextiles.
  • Felt — wool fibres are agitated with heat, moisture and pressure, causing the scales on the wool fibre surface to interlock and mat together. Felt does not fray when cut, making it easy to use for craft projects, hat bodies and industrial filter pads. Synthetic fibre felts mimic this by needle punching rather than scale entanglement.

Knitted Fabrics

Knitted fabrics are made from a single yarn (or multiple yarns) forming interlocking loops. The looped structure gives knitted fabrics their characteristic stretch, comfort and ability to conform to the body. There are two main types:

  • Weft knit — the yarn runs horizontally across the fabric, forming rows of loops. A stitch dropped in one row can cause a ladder to run down the fabric. Weft-knit fabrics stretch in all directions and are used for T-shirts, socks and jumpers. Jersey is the most basic weft-knit structure.
  • Warp knit — multiple yarns run vertically (in the warp direction), with each yarn looping diagonally to interlock with adjacent yarns. Warp-knit fabrics are more stable than weft knits — they are less likely to ladder — and have less stretch. Examples include tricot (used in lingerie and sportswear lining) and lace fabrics.

The forces and stresses a fabric must withstand depend on its end use. A woven fabric has high tensile strength along the warp and weft but very little stretch in those directions — suitable for structures like bags, sails or tailored jackets that must hold their shape. On the bias (45° to the grain), woven fabric has far more stretch and drape, which couture dressmaking exploits. A knitted fabric accommodates stretch in multiple directions because the loops can extend without the yarn itself stretching — making knits ideal for close-fitting activewear and undergarments. A non-woven typically has low tensile strength and minimal stretch but can be very uniform in thickness and density, useful for filtration or single-use medical applications. Designers must match fabric construction to the forces the product will experience in use.

Selecting Textiles by Function, Aesthetics, Cost and Sustainability

When selecting a fabric for a specific product, designers balance multiple criteria simultaneously. Function considers the mechanical and physical performance needed: does the fabric need to be waterproof, fire-retardant, stretch under load, or withstand repeated washing? Aesthetics includes colour, texture, pattern, drape and lustre — how the product looks and feels to the consumer. Cost encompasses fibre price, fabric production cost and the end retail price point the brand is targeting. Availability and lead times affect whether a fabric can be reliably sourced in the required quantities and colours.

Environmental considerations are increasingly significant in fabric selection. Certifications such as GOTS (Global Organic Textile Standard) verify that organic cotton meets environmental and social standards throughout the supply chain. The Higg Index, developed by the Sustainable Apparel Coalition, allows brands to measure and compare the environmental footprint of different materials, helping designers choose fabrics with lower water use, carbon emissions and chemical inputs.

Key Fact

No single fabric is perfect for every application. A designer choosing fabric for a children's raincoat needs waterproofing and durability; for a ballet costume they need lightweight drape and freedom of movement; for a hospital gown they need hygiene, ease of sterilisation and affordability. Context determines the criteria hierarchy.

Thread count refers to the number of warp and weft threads per square inch (or 10 cm) of woven fabric. A higher thread count generally indicates a finer, smoother, more tightly woven fabric — which is why high thread counts are marketed in premium bed linen. However, thread count alone does not determine quality: the fibre type, yarn quality and finishing treatments matter equally. A 200-thread-count sheet made from long-staple Egyptian cotton may feel superior to a 400-thread-count sheet made from short-staple fibre with multi-ply yarns artificially inflating the count. Understanding this helps designers critically evaluate fabric specifications rather than relying on a single marketing number.
exam_tip_html: When asked to compare two fabric construction methods, always relate the structural difference to a practical consequence. For example: 'A weft-knit fabric is made from interlocking loops that can extend under load, so it stretches easily in all directions — making it suitable for a T-shirt where the wearer needs freedom of movement. A plain-weave fabric has yarns interlaced at right angles, giving it stability but very little stretch, making it more suitable for a structured jacket.' Simply naming the difference without linking it to a use or property will not score the higher marks on a 4- or 6-mark question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Woven fabrics (plain, twill, satin) interlace warp and weft at right angles, giving stability and shape-retention; knitted fabrics form interlocking loops that stretch and recover, ideal for close-fitting or comfort garments.
  • Non-woven fabrics are bonded or felted directly from fibres without spinning or weaving; they are cheaper to make but weaker and less drapeable, used in interfacing, felt and disposable products.
  • Fabric selection for any product involves balancing function, aesthetics, cost, availability and environmental impact; context always determines which criteria take priority.

glossary_terms.definition: A continuous twisted strand of fibres produced by spinning; yarns are the building blocks from which fabrics are woven or knitted.
A fabric made on a loom by interlacing two sets of yarns — the warp (running lengthways) and the weft (running widthways) — at right angles to each other.
A knitted structure in which the yarn runs horizontally, forming rows of interlocking loops that stretch in all directions and can ladder if a loop is dropped.
A non-woven fabric made by agitating wool fibres with heat, moisture and pressure so that the scaly surface of the fibres interlocks and mats together permanently.

practice_questions.text:
Which weave structure creates a diagonal rib on the fabric surface?
A) Plain weave
B) Satin weave
C) Twill weave
D) Warp knit
Name the two sets of yarns used to make a woven fabric.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each: warp (yarns running lengthways) and weft (yarns running widthways). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a knitted fabric differs from a woven fabric in terms of its structure and stretch properties.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• A knitted fabric is made from interlocking loops formed from a single yarn, whereas a woven fabric interlaces two sets of yarns (warp and weft) at right angles.
• The looped structure of a knitted fabric allows it to stretch easily in multiple directions.
• A woven fabric is relatively stable and does not stretch significantly along the warp or weft grain. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why felt is used for craft projects rather than woven fabrics, referring to its structure and properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Felt is a non-woven fabric made by matting wool fibres together; its structure means it does not have a warp and weft, so it does not fray when cut.
• This means edges do not need to be hemmed or finished, making it quicker and easier to use for cutting intricate shapes.
• Felt is also relatively inexpensive and available in a range of colours, making it accessible for craft use.
• Its thickness and stiffness allow it to hold a cut shape without curling or distorting.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer would select an appropriate fabric for a high-performance cycling jersey, considering at least three different criteria.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Function: the fabric must have stretch and recovery to allow freedom of movement; a weft-knit structure with elastane would provide this. It should also manage moisture (wick sweat away) to keep the rider comfortable at high exertion levels.
• Function: aerodynamic properties may be needed — a smooth, low-drag surface fabric reduces wind resistance at speed.
• Aesthetics: bright, visually distinctive colours or team livery are important for visibility and branding; the fabric must accept vibrant dye.
• Cost: professional cycling jerseys use high-specification technical fabrics (e.g. engineered polyester-elastane blends), which cost more but the target market (professional or serious amateur cyclists) will pay a premium.
• Environment: a manufacturer might choose recycled polyester (rPET) to reduce environmental impact without compromising performance.
[6 marks — Mastering: Three or more criteria addressed with specific fabric/construction choices and clear justification. Secure: Three criteria named with some development. Developing: Two criteria with limited development. Emerging: One criterion or very vague answer.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of woven fabrics compared with knitted fabrics for a fashion designer producing a range of tailored suits.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of woven fabrics for tailored suits:
• Woven fabrics (e.g. twill-weave wool gabardine) are dimensionally stable — they hold their shape and do not stretch out during wear, essential for a structured jacket silhouette.
• They can be cut and manipulated using tailoring techniques (darts, pad stitching, interfacing) that depend on the fabric not distorting.
• A wide range of yarns, thread counts and weave structures allow the designer to select specific weights and textures for summer or winter wear.
Disadvantages of woven fabrics for tailored suits:
• Woven fabrics fray when cut, requiring all seam allowances and edges to be finished, adding time and cost to construction.
• They offer minimal comfort stretch; a poorly fitted woven suit restricts movement, so fit must be precise.
Advantages of knitted fabrics for tailored suits:
• Knitted fabrics (e.g. ponte knit) offer inherent stretch, meaning the suit is more comfortable across a range of body movements and sizes without needing darts for ease.
• Knit suits are often lighter and more packable, appealing to business travellers.
Disadvantages of knitted fabrics for tailored suits:
• Knits can bag at the knees and elbows and are harder to press into crisp lines, making the garment look less formal over time.
• Many knit structures snag or ladder, shortening the product's life.
[8 marks — Mastering: Balanced, developed discussion with at least two points per side linked clearly to the tailored suit context. Secure: Points identified with some development and reasonable balance. Developing: Listed points, limited context or imbalanced. Emerging: One-sided or superficial.]

knowledge_checks.q: In a woven fabric, what is the term for yarns running lengthways on the loom?
Which fabric construction is most likely to ladder if a single stitch is dropped?
Felt is made by agitating wool fibres with heat, moisture and pressure so that their _____ surfaces interlock permanently.
A satin weave creates a lustrous surface because the warp _____ over four or more weft threads before going under one.
Match each fabric construction to its key property or use:
right: Firm and hard-wearing; yarns alternate over-under in a simple pattern
Stretches in all directions due to interlocking loops; used for T-shirts
Non-woven; does not fray when cut; used for craft and filtration

flashcard_questions.q: What is yarn and how is it made from staple fibres?
flashcard_questions.a: A continuous twisted strand; fibres are carded, drawn out and twisted together by spinning.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three main woven fabric structures?
flashcard_questions.a: Plain weave, twill weave and satin weave.

flashcard_questions.q: How is a twill weave identified on a fabric surface?
flashcard_questions.a: By a diagonal rib created when the weft passes over two or more warp threads before going under one.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does satin-weave fabric have a lustrous surface?
flashcard_questions.a: Long warp floats over four or more weft threads reflect light, creating a smooth, shiny appearance.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes felt different from other non-woven fabrics?
flashcard_questions.a: Felt is made by matting wool fibres with heat, moisture and pressure so their scaly surfaces interlock permanently.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main structural difference between weft knit and warp knit?
flashcard_questions.a: Weft knit: yarn runs horizontally in rows of loops that can ladder. Warp knit: multiple yarns run vertically and interlock diagonally, giving more stability.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do woven fabrics generally hold their shape better than knitted fabrics?
flashcard_questions.a: Interlaced warp and weft yarns resist stretch along their length, giving dimensional stability.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one disadvantage of woven fabrics compared with knitted fabrics?
flashcard_questions.a: Woven fabrics fray when cut, so all edges need finishing; they also have very little comfort stretch.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two criteria a designer considers when selecting a fabric.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: function, aesthetics, cost, availability, environmental impact.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the GOTS certification verify?
flashcard_questions.a: That organic cotton meets environmental and social standards throughout the supply chain.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a knitted fabric suitable for a close-fitting sports top?
flashcard_questions.a: Its looped structure stretches in multiple directions, allowing freedom of movement and a comfortable fit.

flashcard_questions.q: What advantage does needle-punched non-woven interfacing offer a tailor?
flashcard_questions.a: It stiffens and supports collars or waistbands without adding significant weight or bulk.

hero_image_caption: The way fibres are interlaced, looped or bonded together determines everything about how a fabric performs — from a crisp tailored jacket to a stretchy sports top.
